module_title: Open System Topologies - Kernel-Shell Architectures and Terminal Commands
introduction: Tailored for analytical papers like SSC CGL Tier-2 (Mains) and technical Bank IT Officer exams, this advanced module breaks down the layered architectural topology of open systems, defines the BASH command interpreter, and details native command syntax.

core_concepts.title: The Layered Linux Architecture
core_concepts.description:
Linux operates in strict concentric rings of privilege:
1. Hardware: The physical components (CPU, RAM).
2. Kernel: The core software engine that interacts directly with the hardware. It manages memory and process cycles.
3. Shell: The Command Interpreter. It captures text commands typed by the user, translates them, and passes them to the Kernel.
4. Application: The outer layer running user utilities (browsers, scripts).

core_concepts.title: BASH (Bourne Again Shell)
core_concepts.description: The default command-line shell environment for most Unix and Linux distributions. Just as Windows uses Command Prompt (CMD), Linux utilizes the BASH Terminal to execute administrative commands via code.

core_concepts.title: Essential Linux Terminal Commands
core_concepts.description:
- `ls`: Lists all files and directories inside the current folder.
- `pwd` (Print Working Directory): Outputs the absolute path of the directory you are currently standing in.
- `mkdir`: Creates a brand-new directory folder.
- `grep` (Global Regular Expression Print): Scans inside files to locate lines that match a specific text pattern.
- `chmod` (Change Mode): Alters the security access permissions (Read, Write, Execute) of a file.

core_concepts.title: GPL (General Public License)
core_concepts.description: The software license model under which Linux is distributed. It enforces a rule called 'Copyleft'—stating that anyone who modifies Linux and redistributes it must also release their modified source code to the public completely free.

important_entities.name: Root
important_entities.significance: While Windows calls its master profile the 'Administrator', Unix and Linux systems call it the 'Root' user. The Root account holds complete, absolute control over the system configuration and can delete core system directories.

important_entities.name: Headless Environment
important_entities.significance: True enterprise Linux servers operate without any Graphical User Interface (headless). There are no icons or windows; 100% of the administration is managed strictly through text commands via a Shell.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: In Tier-2 statement-based questions, examiners often ask: 'Which component is responsible for interpreting user commands?' Candidates reflexively choose the Kernel. This is a trap. The command interpreter is strictly the 'Shell'. The Kernel only accepts binary system calls from the shell.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: The Specificity of the grep Command
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A highly repeated question in advanced mains papers tests text parsing. If a question asks how to locate a specific string or word *inside* a giant text file using the terminal, the answer is always `grep`.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Path Where I'm Dwelling / Print Working Directory
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: If you get lost in deep, nested command-line folders, type `pwd`. It will immediately print your exact physical directory path on screen.

exam_strategy_tips: In technical specialist officer exams, you may encounter octal notation questions for the `chmod` command (e.g., `chmod 777`). Remember that 7 represents full Read (4) + Write (2) + Execute (1) permissions assigned globally.
